input: In this tutorial passage, the aim is to explain the pump affinity laws, which describe how flow, head, and power respond when the speed of a centrifugal pump is varied. Broadly speaking, the passage presents three proportional relationships. First, flow is proportional to speed. Second, head is proportional to the square of speed. Third, and most dramatically, power is proportional to the cube of speed. These relationships can be thought of as a compact way of summarising what happens to the main performance variables when one operating variable, namely speed, is changed for a centrifugal pump. Flow, in this context, is the delivered volume rate, and it follows speed in direct proportion. Head behaves differently, because it is linked to speed through a squared relationship rather than a simple linear one. Power behaves differently again, because it is linked to speed through a cubed relationship, which means that its response is stronger than the responses of both flow and head. To make this clearer, the passage includes a worked check based on the power relationship. In that check, doubling the speed is shown to multiply the power by 8. The example is useful because it highlights the practical implication of the cubic relationship: even a change that is described simply as a doubling of speed corresponds to a much larger change in power. The multiplier 8 is therefore not an incidental detail; it is the numerical signature of the cubic law in the passage.
target: This tutorial explains how flow, head, and power change when the speed of a centrifugal pump changes. The outcome is stated at the start: flow is proportional to speed, head is proportional to speed squared, and power is proportional to speed cubed. A worked check is included at the close: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. The three proportionalities describe one speed change on one centrifugal pump. Flow is the delivered volume rate in the comparison. When speed changes, the affinity law for flow applies the same proportional change to flow, with no separate correction introduced in the passage. Head is treated through its own proportionality. The square in the head law means that head does not follow the flow law: the relation is stronger than direct proportion because the speed term is squared before the comparison is read. Power has the strongest of the three relations. The cube in the power law is the reason the worked check gives a large multiplier from a doubling of speed. Read together, the laws separate three questions that are often merged. A speed change asks how much flow changes, how much head changes, and how much power changes; the affinity laws answer with direct proportion for flow, a squared proportion for head, and a cubed proportion for power. The worked check uses the power law only. Doubling speed multiplies power by 8, and the check confirms the cubic form of the power relation.
